text: The Jammu division is a revenue and administrative division of the Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in the disputed Kashmir region, bordered by the Kashmir division to the north, Ladakh to the east, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to the south, and the Line of Control to the west, separating it from Pakistani-administered Kashmir. It consists of the districts of Jammu, Doda, Kathua, Ramban, Reasi, Kishtwar, Poonch, Rajouri, Udhampur, and Samba, with most of the land being hilly or mountainous, including the Pir Panjal Range that separates it from the Kashmir Valley and parts of the Great Himalayas in Doda and Kishtwar. The principal river is the Chenab. Jammu city is the largest city in the division and serves as the winter capital of Jammu and Kashmir, known as the "City of Temples" due to its numerous temples and shrines with prominent shikhars. It is a major pilgrimage center for Hindus, with a majority of the population practicing Hinduism, while Islam and Sikhism have strong cultural presence. Historically, the hilly regions south and southwest of the Kashmir Valley formed the Jammu Province of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, comprising 22 hill states during the declining Mughal Empire, known as the Dugar group of states, with "Durgara" being a medieval term linked to the region; the term appears in an 11th-century copper plate inscription from Chamba and is associated with Vallapura or Babbapura, though not mentioned in the Rajatarangini. Jammu is mentioned in Timur’s chronicles from 1398, and Raja Bhim Dev is noted as a supporter of Mubarah Shah against Jasrat, who conquered Jammu in 1423 after killing Bhim Dev and later appointed Manik Dev as a vassal. In the early 16th century, Jammu was described as a powerful state in the Punjab hills, and under Emperor Akbar, the hill kingdoms were brought under Mughal suzerainty with considerable autonomy. After the decline of Mughal power, the Jammu state under Raja Dhruv Dev of the Jamuwal family asserted dominance, reaching its peak under Raja Ranjit Dev (r. 1728–1780), who was widely respected. By the 1770s, the Sikh misls, including the Bhangi, Kanhaiya, and Sukerchakia, gained ascendancy, with the Bhangi misl attacking Jammu and forcing Ranjit Dev into tributary status, and Brij Lal Dev being defeated by Mahan Singh, who sacked and plundered the region. In 1808, Jammu was annexed to the Sikh Empire by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the son of Mahan Singh. Gulab Singh, a descendant of Dhruv Dev, joined the Sikh forces, earned a jagir near Jammu, and was made a hereditary Raja of Jammu in 1822 by Ranjit Singh, with his brother Dhyan Singh receiving Poonch and Chibhal and Suchet Singh receiving Ramnagar. By 1827, Gulab Singh had brought all principalities between Kashmir and Jammu under his control, placing the entire Jammu province under the three Jamwal brothers within the Sikh Empire. After Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s death in 1839, internal conflicts weakened the Sikh court, and Gulab Singh’s brothers and nephew were murdered. During the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–1846), Gulab Singh remained neutral but was later invited to Lahore and installed as prime minister, actions which contributed to a Sikh defeat. The British, seeking to weaken the Sikhs, demanded a war indemnity including all hilly territory between the Ravi and Indus rivers, which was transferred to Gulab Singh for 7.5 million Nanakshahee Rupees, establishing the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under the Dogra dynasty. During Dogra rule, Jammu and Srinagar alternated as capitals, six months to a year each, with Poonch and Chibhal granted as jagirs to Dhyan Singh’s sons, Jawahir Singh and Moti Singh; Jawahir Singh was exiled for conspiracies, Chibhal reverted to Gulab Singh, and Poonch remained under Moti Singh and his descendants under Jammu and Kashmir’s suzerainty. During the partition of India, Maharaja Hari Singh, facing a rebellion in the west and a Pashtun tribal invasion from Pakistan, acceded to India on 26–27 October 1947, after initially refusing to accede to either India or Pakistan due to the region’s mixed religious composition. India airlifted troops to repel the invasion, though major portions of Muzaffarabad, Poonch, and Mirpur remained under Pakistani control, with the rest incorporated into India under Article 370, granting autonomy. The division has eight geographical subregions: Ravi-Tawi Kandi plains, Shiwaliks, Pir Panjal belt, Chenab Valley, Bhaderwah Valley, Gandoh Valley, Paddar Valley, and Warwan-Marwah Valley. The climate varies with altitude: Jammu city has hot summers, rainy monsoons, and mild cold, foggy winters without snowfall, while higher hills are snow-capped; Patnitop is a popular winter resort, and the Vaishno Devi shrine is snow-covered in winter. The Banihal Pass often closes due to heavy snowfall. According to the 2011 census, the total population of Jammu Division is 5,350,811, with Scheduled Castes (Dalits) at 19.44% and Scheduled Tribes at 15–20%. Five districts—Rajouri, Poonch, Doda, Kishtwar, and Ramban—have Muslim majorities, while the southwest plains are predominantly Hindu. The Dogra ethnic group comprises approximately 47% of the population and is closely related to Punjabis. The Jammu district has 84% Hindus, 7% Muslims, and most of the remainder are Sikhs; Hindus are predominant in Jammu, Kathua, Samba, and Udhampur, and roughly half in Reasi. Hindus include native Dogras, Kashmiri Pandits, Punjabi Hindu migrants, and refugees from Kotli and Mirpur. Sikhs are mainly migrants from Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Dogri is spoken by a majority in Jammu, Udhampur, Kathua, Samba, and Reasi, with other languages including Gojri, Pahari, Kashmiri, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu. Hindu castes include 30% Brahmins, 27% Rajputs, 15% Thakkar (combined with Rajputs), 2% Jat, 10% Khatri, and 8% Megh and Chamar; Backward Classes make up 32%. Muslim-majority districts include Poonch and Rajouri, where Gujjar, Bakerwal, and Pahari groups are ethno-linguistically distinct from Kashmiri Muslims, and Kashmiri Muslims are present in Kishtwar, Ramban, Doda, and Reasi. The Jammu division has 10 districts as of April 2021, including Bhimber, Kotli, Mirpur, Poonch (western parts), Haveli, Bagh, and Sudhnati, which are now part of Pakistan-administered Jammu and Kashmir. Major political parties include Congress, BJP, National Conference, Jammu and Kashmir People's Democratic Party, and Jammu and Kashmir National Panthers Party. Various groups, including the BJP, have advocated for the separation of Jammu from Kashmir and its inclusion as a distinct entity in the Indian Union, citing neglect by Kashmir-centric administrations. In November 2020, IkkJutt Jammu was launched as a party demanding Jammu division’s separation and statehood and campaigned against the Roshni Act, declared unconstitutional by the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in 2020. The current legislative assembly structure (46 seats in Kashmir, 37 in Jammu) has been criticized for depriving Jammu of equal decision-making power, leading to repeated demands for a Delimitation Commission; after the state’s reclassification as a Union territory, a commission was established with retired Supreme Court judge Ranjana Prakash Desai as chairman. The Jammu Chamber of Commerce & Industry is the apex body for traders and industrialists in the region. Jammu is known for its landscape, ancient temples, Hindu shrines, Mubarak Mandi Palace, Amar Mahal Palace (now a museum), gardens, and forts. The Vaishno Devi shrine, located 48 km from Jammu in Katra on the Trikuta Hills at 1,700 meters, is a sacred cave shrine 30 meters long and 1.5 meters high, with shrines dedicated to Mahakali, Mahalakshmi, and Mahasarasvati; pilgrims trek 13 km to enter through a narrow opening and walk through icy waters. The shrine is associated with a legend of the goddess hiding from a demon. Purmandal, 35 km from Jammu, is an ancient holy place with Shiva temples and celebrates Shivratri with festive activities. Mansar Lake, 62 km from Jammu, is a 34 km² lake fringed by forest-covered hills, a holy site with legends similar to Lake Manasarovar, and features a shrine to Shesha, a six-headed serpent, with iron chains placed on a boulder; newlyweds perform three circumambulations for blessings. Nearby temples of Umapati Mahadev, Narasimha, and Durga are visited by devotees, and people take holy dips on festivals; certain communities perform the Mundan ceremony here. Boating facilities are provided by the Tourism Department.

Mansar Lake, located at 5.14694°E / 32.69611, is both an excursion destination and a holy site in Jammu, sharing the legend and sanctity of Lake Manasarovar. On the eastern bank of the lake stands a shrine dedicated to Shesha, a mythological snake with six heads, featuring a large boulder with iron chains possibly representing small serpents guarding the deity. Newlyweds perform three circumambulations (Parikarma) around the lake to seek Shesha’s blessings. Nearby are ancient temples of Umapati Mahadev and Narasimha, as well as a temple of Durga, visited by large numbers of devotees who take a holy dip in the lake during festivals. Certain Hindu communities perform the Mundan ceremony (first haircut) of their male children here. The lake offers boating facilities managed by the Tourism Department. With its religious significance and natural heritage, Mansar Lake is popular among tourists due to its flora and fauna. The lake is encircled by an illuminated path with viewing decks for observing seasonal birds, tortoises, and fish species. A nearby wildlife sanctuary houses spotted deer, neelgai, and water birds such as cranes and ducks. Visitors can also witness the traditional lifestyle of Gujjar and Backarwals, who live in open Kullhas in the hills around the lake and wear ethnic costumes. The Mansar Lake road connects to a major route linking Pathankot to Udhampur, a strategically important town on National Highway No. 1A. This by-pass road avoids Jammu city, and Surinsar Lake, linked to Mansar, is 24 km (15 mi) from Jammu via this route. Bahu Fort, situated about 5 km from Jammu city on the left bank of the Tawi river, is one of the oldest forts in the city, originally constructed by Raja Bahulochan over 3000 years ago and later improved by Dogra rulers. Inside the fort is a temple dedicated to Goddess Kali, known as Bave Wali Mata, the presiding deity of Jammu. Pilgrims gather here every Tuesday and Sunday for "Tawi flowing worship," and the fort is now surrounded by a terraced garden that is a favorite picnic spot. Bagh-e-Bahu, a Mughal-age garden on the Tawi riverbank, offers views of the old city and river, with a small canteen on one side. On the by-pass road behind Bahu Fort, the city forest surrounds the ancient Mahamaya Temple overlooking the Tawi river, with a small garden surrounded by woods providing a commanding view of the city. Opposite Bahu Fort, a temple dedicated to Mahamaya, a Dogra-descended goddess who died 14 centuries ago fighting invaders, stands. The present temple, built shortly after Maharaja Gulab Singh’s coronation in 1822 and known as Bawey Wali Mata or Mahakali, is considered second only to Mata Vaishno Devi in mystical power. The Raghunath Temple, located at the city center and built in 1857, was initiated by Maharaja Gulab Singh in 1835 CE and completed by his son Maharaja Ranbir Singh in 1860 CE. The temple’s inner walls are covered with gold on three sides, and it features many galleries with hundreds of thousands of shaligrams. It has seven shrines, each with its own tower, making it the largest temple complex in northern India. Though 130 years old, it boasts one of the richest collections of ancient Sanskrit scriptures and manuscripts in its library. The temple’s architecture blends Mughal influences with gold-plated interiors, and its main sanctuary is dedicated to Lord Rama, the eighth incarnation of Vishnu and the patron deity of the Dogras. The temple also houses a Sanskrit library with rare manuscripts. Along the Tawi river, the Peer Kho Cave temple, believed to be where Ramayana character Jamvant (the bear god) meditated, and the Panchbakhtar and Ranbireshwar temples dedicated to Lord Shiva exist. The Ranbireshwar Temple, located on Shalimar Road near the New Secretariat and built by Maharaja Ranbir Singh in 1883 CE, features a central Shiva lingam measuring 2.3 meters (7 ft 7 in) and twelve crystal lingams ranging from 150 to 380 mm (5.9 to 15.0 in), along with galleries containing thousands of Shiva lingams on stone slabs. The Shivkhori cave shrine, located in Reasi District, depicts a natural shivlingum and is one of the most venerated cave shrines of Lord Shiva in the region. The cave is approximately 150 meters (490 ft) long and contains a 4 ft (1.2 m) high Svayambhu Lingum that constantly bathes in milky lime fluid dripping from the ceiling. The first entrance is wide enough to accommodate 300 devotees at once, and the inner chamber is smaller. The cave contains natural images of various Hindu deities and is known as "the Home of Gods." An annual 3-day Shiv Khori mela is held on Maha Shivratri, usually in February or the first week of March, attracting thousands of pilgrims from across the state and beyond. To manage the growing influx, the Shiv Khori Shrine Board has developed facilities including a Shrine Guest House at Ransoo (cost: Rs. 19 lakh), a reception center and pony shed (cost: ₹7.959 million or US$94,000), tile work on a 3-kilometer-long track, plantation of ornamental and medicinal plants, and park development. Other planned improvements include electrification of the cave with modern systems, oxygen and electric generators, exhaust fans, shelter sheds with toilet facilities near the site, 15 shelter sheds along the route from Ransoo to the cave, a railing from the base camp to the cave, a 15,000/EfnrKing water reservoir, proper sanitation, a 25 kV electric transformer, a clock room, permanent bus services from Katra, Udhampur, and Jammu, a police post, a dispensary, and an STD PCO. Recently, the management of Shiv Khori has been transferred to the Sri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board. The Chandi Maa temple in Machel village, District Kishtwar, is about 290 km (180 mi) from Jammu. During the annual 'Chhadi Yatra' in August, thousands visit the shrine, which was first visited in 1981 by Thakur Kulveer Singh of Bhaderwah. Since 1987, he has organized the Chhadi Yatra annually. Travel agents and private cabs from Jammu, Udhampur, Ramnagar, and Bhaderwah arrange transport; the journey takes about 10 hours by road from Jammu to Gulabgarh, the base camp, with a 32 km foot journey that usually takes two days. People often stay overnight in villages along the way, and roadside 'langers' (free food points) are set up. The government provides basic amenities. A helicopter service from Jammu and Gulabgarh is available, with a helipad just 100 meters (330 ft) from the shrine. Jammu’s major attractions include the revolving restaurant Falak on the top floor of KC Residency hotel, Ragunath Bazar as the main tourist and shopping district, and Gandhi Nagar’s Gole Market on Apsara Road. Green Belt Park along Green Belt Road and Rajinder Park on Canal Road—situated between two canals and featuring a large fountain lit at night with a children’s area—are popular spots. The city has the "Big Bazaar" at Jewel Chowk and shopping malls such as 'Wave - The Wave Mall' and Palm Island near Canal Road. Bahu-Plaza in Trikuta Nagar is a commercial hub and youth hangout, housing most of the corporate sector and mobile phone companies including Airtel, BSNL, Vodafone, Aircel, and Tata Indicom. It also hosts cinema halls such as KC Cineplex, Wave Cinema, Palm Cinema, and a PVR near KC Cineplex. Jammu is known for its food specialties including chocolate barfi, sund panjeeri, patisa, and local dishes like rajma with rice and kalaadi, a processed cheese made with calf rennet in buffalo milk. Fiddlehead fern (kasrod), a GI-tagged item, is highly valued for taste and medicinal properties and is consumed as a vegetable or pickle. Kohlrabi, known as kaddam in Jammu, is another specialty, often eaten with rice. Kalari cheese, made in the Ramnagar region, is famous throughout the state. Dogri food specialties include ambal, khatta meat, kulthein di dal, dal patt, maa da madra, rajma, and auriya. Pickles typical of Jammu include those made from kasrod, girgle, mango with saunf, zimikand, tyaoo, seyoo, and potatoes. Auriya is a potato-based dish, and during weddings, kayoor and sund are prepared. Lohri, celebrated a day before Makar Sankranti, marks the end of Poh (Pausha) month and the beginning of Magha month in the Hindu solar calendar, known as Maghi Sangrand. It is celebrated with traditions such as Chajja making, Hiran Dance, Dandaraas, and preparing Lohri garlands. Children make a peacock replica called Chajja, carry it to houses, and perform a special dance with it, striking sticks in rhythm with drums (Dandaraas). In the hills, a special Hiran Dance is performed where dancers disguise as deer and visit homes with auspicious ceremonies and food. On Lohri, children wear garlands of groundnuts, dry fruits, and candies, and eat Tilcholi—a mixture of sesame, rice, and groundnuts. A pageant of Sassi-Punnu, two lovers from Sindhi folk tradition, is also performed on camels. The next day, Makar Sankranti is celebrated as Uttarain (from Sanskrit: Uttarayana), also called Attrain or Attrani. It is observed on the fourth day of Krishna Paksha of Magha month and is also known as Maghi Sangrand. Dogras observe a tradition of Mansana (charity) of Khichdi of Maah Dal, which is prepared on this day and thus the day is referred to as 'Khichdi wala Parva.' It is also a day for sending food to married daughters. Fairs are held on holy places and pilgrimage sites. People take holy baths in the Devika river and visit pilgrimages like Uttar Behni and Purmandal. This day is also celebrated as the birth anniversary of Baba Ambo ji, a local deity. At the Vasuki temple in Bhaderwah, the idols of Vasuki Nag are covered on Magh Sankranti and uncovered after three months on Vaisakha Sankranti. Sankashti Chaturthi, celebrated on the fourth day of Shukla Paksha of Magha month, is dedicated to Lord Ganesha and is observed by Dogra women who perform Arghya to Chandrama at night, donating and eating Bhugga (Til Jaggery mixture) and radish during the fast. Basant Panchami, dedicated to Goddess Saraswati, is celebrated with yellow, saffron, or orange clothing, saffron-colored food offerings, and folk songs like Aayi Basant and Paala Udant. This day is significant for Dogras as it marks the founding of the Dogri Sanstha in 1944. Gauri Tritiya, observed on the fourth day of Shukla Paksha of Magha month in hill districts like Bhaderwah, Doda, Kishtwar, and Ramban, is similar to Karwa Chauth but involves a fast completed after Gauri Puja. Married women worship Goddess Gauri for the health and longevity of their husbands, and the festivity lasts three days. During this time, women visit neighbors to offer 'Thel' (respect) and receive blessings of 'Suhagan Bho' (live long your husband). Holi is celebrated traditionally in Jammu with Holika Dahan on the eve and color play the next day. Earlier, people used to wear headgears called Patangi made of colored paper and silver ribbons. A Dogra sweet dish, Khaste (similar to Gujjiya), is prepared. A three-day fair is held at Narsingh Dev temple in Kathua. Rama Navami, the birth of Lord Rama, is celebrated with religious fervor and gaiety across Jammu, coinciding with the end of the nine-day Navaratra festival. A special function is held at the Raghunath Temple, where large numbers of devotees offer obeisance to Lord Rama. Even during Dogra rule, the rulers would personally visit the Raghunath Mandir to offer worship to Shri Rama.

Women in Jammu are encouraged to offer ‘Thel’ (respect) to other women and receive in return their blessing ‘Suhagan Bho’ (Live long your husband). Holi is celebrated traditionally in Jammu, with Holika Dahan performed on the eve of the festival, followed by color-playing the next day. Historically, people used to decorate themselves with special headgears called Patangi, made of colored paper and silver ribbons. A Dogra sweet dish named Khaste, similar to Gujjiya, is prepared on this day. A three-day fair is held at the Narsingh Dev temple in Kathua. Rama Navami, marking the birth of Shri Rama, is celebrated with religious enthusiasm and gaiety throughout Jammu and coincides with the culmination of the nine-day Navaratra festival. A special function is held at the historical Raghunath Temple in Jammu city, where many devotees offer obeisance to Lord Rama; even during the Dogra rule, rulers would personally visit the Raghunath Mandir to worship Shri Rama, their patron deity. In addition to worship, discourses on Bhagwan Ram’s life and the Ramayana are conducted. On this occasion, a Shobha Yatra is organized, featuring images of Shri Rama, Mata Sita, and Lakshman, along with tableaux depicting scenes from the Ramayana, which are taken in a grand procession. Devotees shower flower petals on the Yatra, and market unions and Hindu organizations organize Bhandaras. Baisakhi originates from the first month of the Hindu Vikram calendar and is celebrated on the first day of the Vaisakh month, marking Mesha Sankranti; it is also known as 'Basoa' in Dogri. Devotees take a ritual dip in rivers, canals, and ponds early in the morning, and in Dogra households, a Puja is performed afterward, with a portion of the food crop offered to deities. The new fruit of the year is enjoyed on this day. A ritual bath at the Tawi river during Baisakhi is common in Jammu. In Udhampur, Baisakhi is celebrated on the banks of the Devika river, where devotees enjoy folk songs for three days. At Sudhmahadev, the festival is celebrated with great pomp, including a folk song competition and vendors setting up stalls for eatables. Many people visit the Nagbani temple to witness the grand New Year celebration. Baisakhi is considered a harvest festival and is seen as auspicious, especially for marriages. Celebrations include Dogri Bhangra, which is closely related to the Punjabi variant in actions, costumes, and songs. The festival is marked by numerous fairs, with Airwan in Kathua hosting a Baisakhi fair attended by 10,000 people as per the 1961 Census. Around 15,000 pilgrims visit the 700-year-old Subar Nag Devta temple in Bhaderwah every year on Baisakhi. Other Baisakhi fairs are held in Doda Bridge and Ramban. A major festival is held twice a year at the Kali Temple in Bahu Fort. Chaitre Chaudash is celebrated at Uttar Behni and Purmandal, located about 25 km (16 mi) and 28 km (17 mi) from Jammu respectively; Uttar Behni derives its name from the Devak River (locally known as Gupt Ganga) flowing in a northerly direction. Purmandal, 39 km (24 mi) from Jammu city, celebrates Shivratri for three days, marking the marriage of Lord Shiva to Goddess Parvati, with people from Jammu visiting the Peer Khoh Cave Temple, Ranbireshwar Temple, and Panjbhaktar Temple. If one visits Jammu during Shivratri, celebrations are observed almost everywhere. Both Chaitre Chaudash and Shivratri are celebrated similarly. Dhamdeh, also known as Dharma Dhihada or Dharma Divas, is celebrated on the Sankranti of the Aashadha month. People take a ritual bath and perform Mansana (charity) of hand fans, water pitchers, and seasonal fruits like melons, offered in the name of Pitras (ancestors). A major celebration involves offering sweet water drinks and food to the poor and needy. Similar rituals are observed on Nirjala Ekadashi (celebrated on Jyestha Shukla Ekadashi), where a strict Vrata is observed in honor of Lord Vishnu. Rutt Raahde is a festival celebrated by Dogra women of all ages from Aashada Sankranti to Shravana Sankranti, with the last day, Shravana Sankranti, referred to as Sakolade or Minjraan. Young girls and women collect broken earthen pitcher necks, insert seeds of Kharif crops into them, and create Raahde, which are decorated with rangoli patterns using natural colors. Every Sunday, women gather at the site to sing folk songs and enjoy eatables like Rutt, Gheur, and Pudas. On the final day of the festival, Badda Rutt, women assemble again, sing folk songs, enjoy eatables, and immerse the Raahde in water bodies. Shravana Sankranti, also known as Sakolade (named after the ear ornaments worn on this day), is also referred to as Minjraan in parts of Himachal. Janmashtami in Dogri is known as Thongren Da Vrat, meaning a Vrata for Thakur (Lord Krishna). Adults observe a fast in honor of Sri Krishna, while children and youth enjoy kite flying. Girls and women decorate their palms with Teera, a dye from an indigenous plant. Some families keep cereal grains in the name of Kul Devtas, Pitras (ancestors), and family members, known as Deyaa Parna. These grains are offered to the wood of a holy tree called Jhand, known as Jhand Puja. The wood is covered with sacred cloth called shoaath, and clay sculptures of a couple and their children are placed on it and worshipped. They are offered Kheer (without sugar) and Makkhan. Dropads (a type of chapati) are then offered to cows, a practice known as ‘dropad mansnaa’. Some people also enjoy swinging on trees known as peengan. At night, children are dressed up like deities, and towns and cities witness processions. At midnight, Sund Panjeeri is offered as Naivedya to Sri Krishna. Vatsa Dwadashi is celebrated on the twelfth day of Krishna Paksha of Bhadrapada month as Bacch Dua, and Durvashtami on the eighth day of Shukla Paksha of Bhadrapada month as Drubadi. In both festivals, women prepare small-sized idols or sculptures of calves using wheat dough, which are worshipped on water bodies. Soaked black chickpeas and Durva grass are used for Puja, and Dogra dishes like Rutt and Dropad are offered as Naivedya. The festival is celebrated on the first day of the solar month of the Hindu calendar, i.e., Bhadrapada, and holds special significance in the Ramban district of Jammu division. People visit the Chandrabhaga river and offer floral offerings. It is popularly known as Singh Sankrant and is locally traced to the Pandavas. Tulsi Puja is performed in Dogra families from Kartika Shukla Ekadashi to Kartika Purnima, a five-day period known as Panj Bhikham (Bhishma Panchak). During Tulsi Puja, families decorate the Tulsi plant pot and write 'Ram Ram' on it, known as Tulsi Da Chauntra in Dogri. The plant is covered with a Red Dupatta or Chunni. A fast is observed on Kartika Shukla Ekadashi in honor of Lord Vishnu and Tulsi Mata. Women light Diyas from Ekadashi to Purnima on the Tulsi plant, a ceremony known as Deeve in Dogri. Some families may also organize a Tulsi Vivah with Shaligram, as it is believed that Tulsi has affinity with Shaligram. An annual fair is held in honor of Baba Jitto, a simple and honest farmer who committed suicide rather than submit to unjust demands of a local landlord to part with his crop, having died in the village of Jhiri, 14 km from Jammu. A legend has grown around Baba Jitto, and his followers gather at Jhiri on the appointed day from across North India, revere him for his compassion, courage, and honesty. Though the pilgrimage to Mata Vaishno Devi is a year-round event, a visit during the Navratras is considered the most auspicious. To highlight regional culture, heritage, and traditions, the State Tourism Department has instituted the Navratri Festival as an annual event during September or October for the nine auspicious days of the Navratras. A large number of tourists visit the shrine during this period, showcasing religious traditions and popular culture. An eight-day fair is held at the Narsingh and Annapurna temples in Ghagwal of Samba district, involving a procession of the deity on a chariot, known as Rath Kharda Mela. Thousands of devotees from neighboring states like Punjab and Himachal Pradesh and other parts of Jammu attend. People from hilly areas such as Basohli, Doda, Kishtwar, Bani, and Dudu Basantgarh set up stalls to sell handicrafts and woolen items like Pattus, blankets, and shawls. During the fair, the temple is decorated with flowers and lights. Devotees visit to pay obeisance to Bhagwan Narsimha, and a Bhandara is organized. Local farmers sow their fields in the name of Bhagwan Narsimha and offer a portion of the harvest to the temple during the fair. Besides Ghagwal, the Rath Kharda Mela is also held in Ramgarh tehsil of Udhampur district, Parnala village in Billawar tehsil, and Hatli village in Kathua. Shivaratri, meaning 'Shiva's night,' is a significant festival for Hindus, especially those of Kashmiri origin in Jammu. On this day, Lord Shiva and his spouse Parvati are worshipped with great devotion. Esoterically, it symbolizes the mystic union of Jiva (individual soul) with Paramatma (the Supreme Godhead), representing spiritual realization where the world of relativity fades and perfect peace prevails. Alongside worship, social and cultural gatherings are observed, with people rejoicing and exchanging greetings. Jammu region has several institutes offering higher education, ranging from medical and engineering colleges to government and private colleges.
